props.title: Rain Man
props.initialSlug: Autistic savant changes his selfish brother's life

sections.content: Rain Man revolutionized Hollywood's portrayal of autism through Dustin Hoffman's meticulous performance as Raymond Babbitt. The film's road trip structure brilliantly frames the evolving relationship between Raymond and his self-centered brother Charlie (Tom Cruise), avoiding melodramatic clichés for authentic character development. Director Barry Levinson crafts intimate moments that showcase Raymond's abilities and challenges without exploitation, while questioning society's treatment of neurodivergent individuals. This sparked a wave of more nuanced disability representations like What's Eating Gilbert Grape (1993) and I Am Sam (2001).

sections.content: The late 1980s marked a crucial shift in disability representation onscreen. While One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest (1975) examined institutional abuse and The Elephant Man (1980) challenged Victorian-era prejudices, Rain Man brought unprecedented authenticity to mainstream audiences. Hoffman spent a year researching autism, studying with specialists and people with autism to avoid caricature. This dedication influenced later actors like Claire Danes in Temple Grandin (2010) and Eddie Redmayne in The Theory of Everything (2014).

The film's Oscar success - winning Best Picture, Director, Actor, and Original Screenplay - proved audiences would embrace complex stories about disability. This opened doors for films like A Beautiful Mind (2001) and Still Alice (2014), which tackle mental illness and neurological conditions with similar depth. The road movie format, allowing Raymond and Charlie's relationship to develop organically through shared experiences, became a template for character-driven disability narratives. movies.title: Temple Grandin

sections.content: Rain Man transformed the family drama genre by avoiding easy sentimentality. Charlie's journey from seeing Raymond as a meal ticket to genuine brotherhood feels earned through small moments - counting cards in Vegas, sharing routines, navigating Raymond's needs. This influenced films like The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time (2012) and Keep the Change (2017), which similarly balance humor, heart, and authenticity in portraying neurodivergent characters.
